summary: This Best Current Practice describes a way to let a TCP server accept a new connection from a client even when an old connection between the same two endpoints is still in the TIME-WAIT state. It relies on the TCP Timestamps option to tell old packets from new ones. Only the handling of incoming SYN segments in TIME-WAIT changes, which allows faster reconnection.

plainLanguage.summary: After a phone call ends, you normally wait a bit before calling the same person again in case of late echoes. Timestamps let you tell old echoes from new words, so you can call back sooner.

subtitle: How a TCP server can safely accept a new connection from a client while the old one is still in TIME-WAIT.

tldr.problem: When a client reuses the same four-tuple while the server still holds the old connection in TIME-WAIT, the new connection request can fail and time out.
tldr.mechanism: The server compares the timestamp in the incoming SYN with the last timestamp seen on the old connection, and falls back to sequence numbers when timestamps are not in use. If the new values are higher, it honors the SYN.
tldr.outcome: Connections can be re-established faster. If the heuristics fail, the result is no worse than before: the SYN is silently dropped.

today: RFC 6191 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 159). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It only changes how SYNs are handled in TIME-WAIT, and leaves every other TCP state as is.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 6191 builds on the TCP Timestamps option from RFC 1323. That option lets a TCP put a timestamp in its segments for two jobs: Round-Trip Time Measurement (RTTM) and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS).

PAWS needs timestamps to increase on a connection. Nothing requires them to increase across separate connections. But if they do increase across connections between the same two endpoints, they can also help decide what to do with a SYN that arrives while the matching four-tuple is in the TIME-WAIT state. This RFC calls that a heuristic for allowing a new incarnation of the connection.

The idea extends how Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs) were already used for this purpose, as allowed by RFC 1122, and the RFC notes it is already in a number of TCP implementations, such as the Linux kernel.
sections.plainLanguage: Timestamps already help TCP keep its words in order. This memo says the same clock can also help decide whether a new call from an old friend is really new.

sections.title: The Reuse Problem
sections.content:
A client may try to open a new incarnation of a previous connection while the server still has the same four-tuple in TIME-WAIT. This can happen when ephemeral port numbers are reused too quickly, because of a bad port selection policy or simply a high connection rate to the service. In that case, creating the new connection would fail.

RFC 1122, Section 4.2.2.13, already says the request may be accepted if the incoming SYN's sequence number is greater than the last sequence number seen on the previous incarnation. The goal is to stop the sequence number spaces of old and new connections from overlapping, so old segments are not mistaken for new ones.

Many implementations use only this sequence number check. RFC 793 says the ISN generator should be incremented roughly once every four microseconds, which is roughly 250,000 times per second. So a connection that transfers more than 250,000 bytes at more than 250 kilobytes per second can leave a last sequence number above the ISN of a new SYN. The check then fails and the request usually times out. Adding timestamps greatly relaxes these constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: If you hang up and instantly redial, the other side may still be waiting for late echoes and ignore you. Counting only words can fail when you talked a lot. A clock makes it easier.

sections.title: How Incoming SYNs Are Processed
sections.content:
Only SYN segments that arrive for a connection in TIME-WAIT are handled differently. Processing in all other states is unchanged. The RFC says processing SHOULD work as follows.

If the previous incarnation used Timestamps:

  • If Timestamps would be enabled for the new incarnation and the SYN's timestamp is greater than the last timestamp seen on the old one, honor the request (creating a connection in SYN-RECEIVED).
  • If Timestamps would be enabled and the timestamp is equal to the last one, honor the request only when the SYN's sequence number is greater than the last sequence number seen on the old one.
  • If Timestamps would not be enabled, honor the request only when the sequence number is greater than the last one.
  • Otherwise, silently drop the SYN, leaving the old connection in TIME-WAIT.

If the previous incarnation did not use Timestamps, the request is honored when Timestamps would be enabled for the new one, or when they would not be but the sequence number is greater. Otherwise it is silently dropped.

"Timestamps would be enabled" means the SYN carries a Timestamps option and the SYN/ACK the server would send back would carry one too. The "last sequence number" means the one matching the FIN flag of the old connection, not simply the last value seen in the Sequence Number field.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the clock on the new call. If it reads later than the clock on the old call, it picks up. If the clocks match, it checks the word count. Otherwise it stays quiet.

sections.title: Interaction With Timestamp Generation
sections.content:
The algorithm works best when timestamps keep increasing across connections to the same endpoint. This matters most for the TCP that performs the active open, because its timestamps are the ones the algorithm checks. Implementing the algorithm does not by itself place a requirement on how other TCP implementations generate timestamps.

In the worst case, a SYN for a new incarnation carries a timestamp smaller than the last one seen. The heuristics fail and the SYN is ignored, as specified in RFC 1337. The connection request then times out or is accepted after later SYN retransmissions. The RFC says this is no worse than the current state of affairs.

Some stacks do not make timestamps increase across connections. One example is the scheme in RFC 4987 and a referenced post, which allows extended TCP SYN cookies. The RFC notes that this could coexist with monotonic timestamps for the active-open side. It also says OpenBSD's timestamp randomization may prevent this mechanism from recycling TIME-WAIT connections.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone's clock jumps around, the trick just does not work for them, and things go back to how they were. Nothing gets worse.

sections.title: Interaction With ISN Generation
sections.content:
RFC 793 suggests generating ISNs from a global timer so they increase across connections. That makes ISNs predictable, with well-known security implications. RFC 1948 proposes a scheme that still increases across connections but is not easily predictable by an off-path attacker.

Some stacks, notably OpenBSD, randomize ISNs so they do not increase across connections. The RFC cites a source saying this breaks BSD's improved handling of SYNs in TIME-WAIT.

With this document's mechanism, TIME-WAIT recycling can still work when ISNs do not increase, except when the timestamp in the incoming SYN equals the last timestamp seen on the old connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems pick random starting numbers to be safe from sneaky guessers. That breaks the old counting trick, but the clock trick still works in most cases.

sections.title: Security and the Reboot Case
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single pointer: a separate document, "Security Assessment of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)", discusses the security implications of TCP Timestamps and of different timestamp generation algorithms.

Appendix A covers a host that reboots, keeps its IP address and loses its memory of earlier timestamps. RFC 793 already says hosts must not make new connections for 2*MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime) after boot, the "quiet time" idea, so this should not happen. A host that ignores quiet time might send a SYN whose timestamp is not higher, and then the algorithm cannot recycle the old connection. That is the same as having no algorithm at all.
sections.plainLanguage: If a computer forgets its clock after a restart, the trick cannot help it. It should have waited a bit anyway.
